extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Kantian philosophy; philosophers and educated general readers interested in metaphysics, teleology, and moral argumentation
extracted.subtask_description: Articulating and evaluating arguments that ground the concepts of God, freedom, and immortality via moral (practical) Reason and teleology, and distinguishing these from purely theoretical proofs. Emphasis on Kantian distinctions between theoretical cognition and practical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of faith (practical/moral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith ... is trust in the attainment of a design, the promotion of which is a duty, but the possibility of the fulfilment of which (and consequently also that of the only conditions of it thinkable by us) is not to be comprehended by us. Faith, then, that refers to particular objects, which are not objects of possible knowledge or opinion ... is quite moral. It is a free belief, not in that for which dogmatical proofs for the theoretically determinant Judgement are to be found, or in that to which we hold ourselves bound, but in that which we assume on behalf of a design in accordance with laws of freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes moral/practical faith from credulity and theoretical belief; faith is grounded in Reason insofar as Reason is practically employed and is 'adequate for its design' even though not theoretically provable. Use this to justify belief in supersensible objects for practical ends (religion/moral life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: incredulous vs unbelieving vs dogmatical unbelief vs doubtful faith
rubrics_metrics.description: To be incredulous means to cling to maxims, and not to believe testimony in general; but he is unbelieving, who denies all validity to rational Ideas, because there is wanting a theoretical ground of their reality. A dogmatical unbelief cannot subsist together with a moral maxim dominant in the mental attitude ... but a doubtful faith can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinctions to evaluate attitudes toward rational Ideas: incredulity (practical skepticism about testimony), unbelief (rejection of rational ideas for lack of theoretical grounds), dogmatic unbelief (incompatible with moral commitment), and doubtful faith (compatible with moral action despite lack of speculative proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for moral attitude: practical belief to avoid wavering
rubrics_metrics.description: Without [practical faith], the moral attitude of thought in its repudiation of the claim of the theoretical Reason for proofs ... has no permanence; but wavers between practical commands and theoretical doubts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that practical belief (faith) is necessary to stabilize moral commitment when speculative proofs are unavailable; when producing or evaluating moral-theological claims, ensure they supply a practicable conviction that supports duty-bound action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of theoretical cognition of the supersensible
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus the ground of the failure of the attempt to prove God and immortality by the merely theoretical path lies in this, that no cognition whatever is possible of the supersensible in this way (of natural concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical categories and empirical predicates cannot yield determinate concepts of supersensible beings; do not expect theoretical proofs (ontological/cosmological) to deliver knowledge of God, freedom, or immortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral path as source of determinate predicates for supersensible
rubrics_metrics.description: The ground of its success by the moral way (of the concept of freedom) is as follows. Here the supersensible (freedom) ... not only supplies material for cognition of other supersensibles (the moral final purpose and the conditions of its attainability), but also establishes its reality in actions as a fact; though at the same time it can furnish a valid ground of proof in no other than a practical point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing for God or immortality, ground claims in the practical (moral) use of Reason: freedom and moral final purpose provide predicates that find objective reality in moral action, not in theoretical demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: All belief must be grounded on facts: theoretical knowledge vs practical faith
rubrics_metrics.description: All belief must in the first place be grounded upon facts, if it is not to be completely groundless; and therefore the only distinction in proofs that there can be is that belief in the consequence derived therefrom can either be grounded on this fact as knowledge for theoretical cognition, or merely as faith for practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of arguments should ask whether the grounding fact is empirical/theoretical (yielding knowledge) or practical/moral (yielding faith). Avoid conflating these two kinds of grounding when assessing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of ontological and cosmological proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The ontological proof ... concludes from the concept of the Being the most real of all, its absolutely necessary existence ... The other (metaphysico-cosmological) concludes from the necessity of the existence somewhere of a thing ... its complete determination as that of a Being the most real of all. ... Neither proof ... could ever pass from the schools into the world, or have the slightest influence on the mere sound Understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ontological and cosmological arguments skeptically: they rely on conceits about concepts being completely determinate and thus cannot convincingly establish a determinate original Being for common understanding or moral purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical (physico-) teleological proof: limited scope and reliance on moral ground
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof, which rests on a natural concept that can only be empirical and yet is to lead us beyond the bounds of nature ... is that derived from the purposes of nature. ... It produces a similar effect in the way of conviction upon the common Understanding as upon the subtlest thinker. ... But the physico-teleological proof convinces ... because it mingles itself unnoticed with that moral ground of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical teleology (design in nature) can suggest an intelligent Author but cannot by itself yield a determinate theological concept; its persuasive force often depends on covert moral presuppositions. When using/designing teleological arguments, make explicit any moral premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral teleology's superiority for Theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Teleology ... leads to that which is requisite for the possibility of a Theology, viz. to a determinate concept of the supreme Cause, as Cause of the world according to moral laws, and, consequently, to the concept of such a cause as satisfies our moral final purpose. For this are required ... Omniscience, Omnipotence, Omnipresence, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the aim is a concept of God adequate for religion, prioritize moral-teleological grounds: they provide the determinate attributes (as required by moral final purpose) necessary for a theological concept usable in moral life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theology's role: subsidiary to Religion (moral use of Reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: If it be asked why it is incumbent upon us to have any Theology at all, it appears clear that it is not needed for the extension or correction of our cognition of nature or in general for any theory, but simply in a subjective point of view for Religion, i.e. the practical or moral use of our Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess theological claims with their functional role in mind: theology is justified insofar as it supports the moral life (religion) rather than expanding theoretical knowledge of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories only apply to possible experience; can't cognize God theoretically
rubrics_metrics.description: All Categories, which can have no significance for cognition in a theoretical aspect, if they are not applied to objects of possible experience. ... if I think a supersensible Being (God) as the first mover, and thus by the category of causality ... I must not think it as existing in any place in space nor as extended; I must not even think it as existing in time or simultaneously with other beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply empirical categories (causality, space, time, extension) as if they yielded theoretical knowledge of supersensible beings. Use them only analogically and recognize the resulting concepts are empty theoretically but may have practical import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analogy: ascribing attributes to God only analogically for practical ends
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the analogy of an Understanding I can in a certain other aspect think a supersensible being, without at the same time meaning thereby to cognise it theoretically; viz. if this determination of its causality concerns an effect in the world, which contains a design morally necessary but unattainable by a sensible being. ... An Ethical Theology is therefore possible; ... a Theological Physic would be a nonentity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing properties (understanding, omniscience, omnipotence) to God do so by analogy grounded in moral demands: such attributions are valid only for the practical (ethical) reference, not as theoretical knowledge of God's metaphysical constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness and perfection of the original Being cannot be inferred from empirical teleology alone
rubrics_metrics.description: You infer, from the great purposiveness of natural forms and their relations, a world-cause endowed with Understanding; but what is the degree of this Understanding? ... you cannot infer the Almightiness of its Author from so small a standard, and so on. Now you arrive in this way at no definite concept of an original Being available for a Theology; for this can only be found in the concept of the totality of perfections compatible with intelligence, and you cannot help yourself to this by merely empirical data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that empirical design arguments yield a unique, all-perfect deity; any move to uniqueness or maximal perfection requires an arbitrary addition or moral grounding. Make explicit when empirical evidence is being supplemented by non-empirical assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral requirement for duties to be genuine: laws must come from Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: A Theological Ethic (of pure Reason) is impossible; for laws which Reason itself does not give and whose observance it does not bring about as a pure practical faculty, can not be moral. In the same way a Theological Physic would be a nonentity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing moral-theological systems, ensure that moral laws are rooted in practical Reason itself; externally imposed divine ordinances that Reason does not endorse cannot properly be moral laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropologico-teleological observation about desires as representing causal reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Although in such fantastic desires we are conscious of the inadequacy (or even the unsuitability) of our representations for being causes of their objects, yet their reference as causes, and consequently the representation of their causality, is contained in every wish; and this is specially evident if the wish is an affection or longing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this account to explain why humans entertain vain desires: desires exhibit a representation of causal efficacy even when known to be impossible. This anthropological point supports teleological readings of human behavior and the practical necessity of testing powers by action.
